newsitem.title: USA: Senate reverses decline in U.S. foreign aid budget.
newsitem.headline: Senate reverses decline in U.S. foreign aid budget.

text.p: The Senate on Thursday boosted U.S. foreign aid by $1 billion next year and used the annual funding to send messages on domestic and foreign policy issues to Russia, Egypt, Cambodia and other countries.

The Senate approved the $13.2 billion foreign aid package for fiscal 1998, which starts Oct. 1, on a strong bipartisan vote of 91-8. The increase comes after a 60 percent decline in aid over the past decade, but the funds still amounts to less than 1 percent of the federal budget.
The spending bill also provides $3.5 billion requested by the administration for Export-Import Bank loans to U.S. companies.

"American assistance is geared to behaviour," Foreign Operations subcommittee Chairman Mitch McConnell told the Senate as he argued for a variety of provisions he said would be used to further U.S. goals in other countries.

While the Kentucky Republican stated his strong support for the use of U.S. foreign assistance as a constructive alternative to military operations abroad, he warned recipient countries that his panel would review each year whether the money was helping meet U.S. goals.
"Foreign assistance is not an entitlement. It is not something you get automatically this year because you got it last year," McConnell said.

The senior Democrat on the Foreign Relations Committee, Sen. Joe Biden of Delaware, praised the increase and said it would help Washington better further democracy, free trade and human rights abraod.

The bill is $116 million less than President Clinton requested, but during the debate the Senate approved by a 95-4 vote a Republican-sponsored amendment that cuts off funds to Russia if its proposed restrictions on religious freedom became law and to Cambodia if it does not freely and fairly elect its government. Funds for Russia are also contingent on Moscow halting aid for Iran's nuclear programme.
The Senate rejected 60-38 a Clinton administration plan to end the annual certification process by which countries are deemed to be fighting drugs and thus qualify for U.S. aid.
Showing the continued U.S. opposition to the Castro government, the Senate refused to allow Cuban-Americans to send up to $200 a month to family members in Cuba.

In response to North Korea's firing on South Korean troops July 17, the Senate voted to hold back $14 million for the Korean Economic Development Organisation for building two nuclear reactors until the president can certify no armistice violations have occurred for nine months.

As usual, Israel and Egypt will receive the bulk of U.S. aid. Israel was given $3 billion and, after McConnell agreed Egypt had renewed its efforts to further peace in the Middle East, $2.1 billion was set aside for Cairo.
The bill also includes $150 million in economic aid for Jordan.

Eastern Europe and the Baltic states were given $485 million and $800 million was set out for the states of the former Soviet Union. Half of the $225 million for the Ukraine depends on a certification by the White House regarding economic reforms and the country's work to end corruption.
The Senate agreed no U.S. aid should go to the Democratic Republic of the Congo until President Laurent Kabila cooperates with international investigation of alleged mass killings of Hutus.
